RGTI vs QUBT: Which Quantum Computing Stock Has More Upside Potential?
The quantum computing race is no longer just about who can build the most powerful machine. It is increasingly becoming a contest between companies pursuing different paths to commercial adoption while convincing investors they can turn breakthrough technology into sustainable businesses.
That contrast was on full display during the latest earnings season as Rigetti Computing RGTI and Quantum Computing Inc. QUBT outlined sharply different strategies for scaling their businesses. Rigetti doubled down on its superconducting quantum computing roadmap, highlighting progress on its 108-qubit Cepheus-1 system, a modular chiplet architecture aimed at 1,000-qubit systems and growing government-backed initiatives. Meanwhile, QUBT leaned into its room-temperature photonic platform, expanding through acquisitions, semiconductor manufacturing and AI-focused photonics products designed to generate commercial revenue alongside its long-term quantum ambitions.
Both companies reported second-quarter revenues above $5 million, but the drivers behind those results looked very different. Rigetti's 185% revenue jump was fueled by quantum hardware deployments, while QUBT's 9,000% surge reflected contributions from its rapidly expanding photonics and semiconductor businesses. With both stocks competing for investor attention in one of the market's fastest-evolving industries, the bigger question is which execution strategy appears stronger based on their latest updates.
Let's get into more detail.
Rigetti's second-quarter results reinforced an execution-driven investment case as revenues jumped 185% year over year to $5.1 million, fueled by on-premises Novera QPU sales, while gross margin expanded to 43% from 31% a year ago.
Beyond the financials, the company continued advancing its 108-qubit Cepheus-1 platform, reaffirmed its chiplet-based roadmap toward roughly 1,000 qubits over the next three years, strengthened its government ties through a U.S. Department of Commerce letter of intent for up to $100 million in potential CHIPS Act funding and ended the quarter with $541.3 million in cash, cash equivalents and investments and no debt.
Rigetti's biggest challenge remains converting technical milestones into durable commercial scale. Although revenues grew sharply, quarterly sales remain relatively modest at $5.1 million, while operating expenses climbed to $30.3 million as the company continued investing heavily in R&D, chip design, fabrication and refrigeration infrastructure to support higher-qubit systems.
At the same time, management still needs to deliver meaningful improvements in Cepheus-1's gate fidelity and coherence times before progressing toward its 1,000-qubit ambitions, while the proposed CHIPS Act funding remains contingent on a definitive agreement and customary approvals.
Quantum Computing's second quarter highlighted a broader commercialization strategy that extends beyond quantum computing alone. Revenues surged to $5.6 million from just $61,000 a year ago, with contributions from government, commercial and educational customers across its photonics portfolio.
The company accelerated its expansion through the acquisitions of NHanced Semiconductors, Luminar Semiconductor and NuCrypt, strengthening its advanced packaging and semiconductor manufacturing capabilities while launching its Fab 2 initiative.
Commercial traction also improved with the rollout of the NeuraWave photonic AI platform, the installation of a DIRAC-3 optimization system at a global consulting firm, a multi-unit NeuraWave framework agreement with Planck Dynamics and a contract backlog that reached $42.5 million, backed by a cash and investment position of roughly $1.3 billion.
QUBT's rapid expansion also brings meaningful execution risks as the company integrates multiple acquisitions while scaling manufacturing and commercialization simultaneously. Operating expenses more than doubled to $21.8 million, due to higher R&D spending, personnel costs, sales and marketing investments and acquisition-related expenses.
The company remains heavily dependent on government-funded work, with management indicating that roughly 70%-80% of current business comes from government subcontracting, while contract timing remains lumpy and backlog is expected to be recognized over 12 to 18 months rather than translating into immediate revenue.
In addition, management is evaluating another $50-$100 million of potential investment to enhance NHanced's manufacturing capabilities, adding another layer of capital deployment and integration complexity.
The Zacks Consensus Estimate for RGTI's 2026 bottom line is pegged at a loss of 19 cents per share, implying a 70.3% improvement over the 2025 reported figure.
The Zacks Consensus Estimate for QUBT's 2026 bottom line is pegged at a loss of 19 cents per share, implying a 72.7% decline over the 2025 reported loss.
Based on short-term price targets offered by six analysts, the average price target for QUBT represents an increase of 103.8% from the last closing price of $9.16.
Based on short-term price targets offered by 11 analysts, the average price target for RGTI represents an increase of 79.1% from the last closing price of $16.50.
Final Take: RGTI or QUBT?
The latest earnings season highlighted two very different execution stories. QUBT paired revenue growth with expanding commercial traction through acquisitions, a growing photonics business, a $42.5 million backlog and a sizeable $1.3 billion cash position, while Rigetti's quarter centered on advancing its superconducting roadmap, government partnerships and long-term technology milestones. Analyst sentiment also reflects a wider upside outlook for QUBT, with its average price target implying 103.8% upside from recent levels compared with 79.1% for Rigetti.
The two stocks entered the next phase with different outlooks. QUBT currently carries a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold), reflecting a more balanced near-term earnings outlook, while Rigetti carries a Zacks Rank #5 (Strong Sell), indicating weaker earnings expectations. Although QUBT appears better positioned from a commercialization and analyst-sentiment standpoint, both companies remain high-risk plays in an emerging industry where execution, customer adoption and technology milestones will likely remain the key factors to watch.

IonQ (IONQ -1.83%) and Rigetti Computing (RGTI -0.66%) are taking entirely different technological routes in their efforts to build useful quantum computers.
IonQ uses trapped-ion technology, where individual charged atoms held in place by precise electromagnetic fields serve as qubits, the basic units of information in any quantum computer. Rigetti Computing uses superconducting qubits, which are tiny electrical circuits cooled to extremely low temperatures.
Image source: Getty Images.
IonQ has demonstrated more than 99.99% fidelity, or accuracy, for 2-qubit gates (operations performed on 2 qubits at the same time). Rigetti Computing has reported roughly 99.1% median 2-qubit fidelity on its 108-qubit Cepheus system. Hence, its typical 2-qubit operation succeeds about 99.1% of the time.
While IonQ may appear to be the obvious technology winner, these figures are not directly comparable. IonQ's 99.99% result came from testing a particular 2-qubit operation, rather than measuring the overall performance of a large commercial quantum computer. A more comparable measure comes from IonQ's Forte systems, which have reported a median 2-qubit fidelity of 99.3% to 99.5%. Hence, although IonQ's qubits still appear to perform operations more accurately than Rigetti Computing's, the gap in accuracy between them is much smaller.
That narrower accuracy gap could prove crucial when quantum calculations become more complex. Using the more comparable figures above, 99.5% fidelity implies an error rate of roughly 0.5%, compared with about 0.9% at 99.1%. Hence, Rigetti Computing's error rate is roughly 1.8 times as high in this comparison.
$17BMarket cap calculated using publicly traded shares outstanding only. Does not include unlisted, private, or dual-class non-traded shares. Implied market cap may vary.
IonQ also has an advantage in how its qubits communicate. The company's trapped-ion systems offer all-to-all connectivity, meaning any qubit can directly interact with another qubit in the system.
Quantum computers with more limited connectivity may need additional operations, known as SWAP gates, to move quantum information between qubits that cannot directly interact. These extra operations can introduce more errors.
IonQ's connectivity can therefore reduce the number of operations needed for some quantum calculations. This can partly offset IonQ's slower quantum gates, which are the basic operations performed on qubits. In one published comparison, IonQ's Forte systems took about 950 microseconds for a 2-qubit gate, while Rigetti Computing's 108-qubit Cepheus system performed such gates in about 60 nanoseconds.
IonQ also needs to prove that the advantages of trapped-ion technology persist as its quantum computers become larger. The company's next-generation Superion 256 platform is designed around 256 qubits. IonQ has already manufactured 256-qubit Superion processor chips at SkyWater, the semiconductor foundry it acquired in July. The company has also successfully trapped ions on prototype versions of the system. However, these systems are not yet being delivered to customers; commercial deliveries are expected to begin in 2027.
In short, the Superion 256 is an important milestone, but the real test for IonQ will be whether its hardware can maintain high accuracy and connectivity as the number of qubits increases.
IonQ has also made progress in quantum error correction, which combines multiple physical qubits to create more reliable logical qubits. In one experiment, the company used 18 physical qubits to encode 4 logical qubits. Some of those logical qubits preserved quantum information for about as long as, or slightly longer than, the individual physical qubits. Researchers call this breakeven performance. This is still far from a fault-tolerant quantum computer, but it shows that IonQ has begun demonstrating its error-correction approach on actual hardware rather than only through simulations.
DARPA -- the U.S. Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency -- has also advanced IonQ to Stage B of its Quantum Benchmarking Initiative. At this stage, the agency is evaluating the company's development plan, technical risks, and the prototypes needed to reduce those risks.
Rigetti Computing's quantum computing technology
Rigetti's much faster quantum computing operations could give it a major advantage if it can improve accuracy while building larger systems.
$5.1BMarket cap calculated using publicly traded shares outstanding only. Does not include unlisted, private, or dual-class non-traded shares. Implied market cap may vary.
The company has already made progress on the scale front. Its 108-qubit Cepheus system combines 12 interconnected 9-qubit chiplets into a 108-qubit processor. Chiplets are smaller processor blocks that can be connected to build larger systems. Rigetti Computing says this approach can help it increase the qubit counts of its quantum computers while avoiding the manufacturing complexities of building increasingly large chips.
However, Rigetti Computing has reported a median 2-qubit fidelity of 99.8% on its 9-qubit system and 99.6% on its 36-qubit system. The figure fell to roughly 99.1% on the 108-qubit Cepheus system. So while it has demonstrated that it can build larger quantum computers, maintaining accuracy as qubit count increases remains a challenge.
Management has set a goal of developing a system with roughly 1,000 qubits, 99.9% 2-qubit fidelity, and 2-qubit operations that take less than 50 nanoseconds, and given itself a timeline of approximately three years. If Rigetti Computing can build a single quantum computer that achieves all of those milestones, its combination of speed, accuracy, and scale could significantly narrow the gap between its tech and IonQ's.
Which company has the technology edge?
I think IonQ has the technology edge today. The company has moved beyond building more physical qubits to demonstrating error correction on actual hardware.
However, its lead is not secure. The Superion 256 is still in the prototype stage. IonQ still needs to prove that its accuracy and connectivity can hold up as its systems become much larger. Rigetti Computing could narrow the gap if it improves accuracy while preserving its existing advantages in speed and scalability.

Rigetti Computing vs. SoundHound AI: Which Tech Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?
Is the future of computing quantum or conversational? Investors deciding between Rigetti Computing (NASDAQ:RGTI) and SoundHound AI (NASDAQ:SOUN) must choose which high-growth technology offers the better long-term potential for their portfolios.
Rigetti is a pioneer in building superconducting quantum computers, while SoundHound provides voice-enabled artificial intelligence software for diverse industries. They are being compared because both represent small-cap bets on the next generation of artificial intelligence, though they operate at opposite ends of the hardware and software spectrum.
Rigetti sells superconducting quantum processors and cloud-based quantum services to research and commercial clients. The company remains a pioneer among tech stocks, particularly within the nascent quantum hardware industry. It serves customers through its Quantum Cloud Services platform, targeting complex problems in fields like climate simulation and drug discovery. Major partners include Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) and Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT), which provide broad cloud access to its hardware. Significant government clients like DARPA also utilize its technology, and such customer concentration adds a layer of risk to the business.
In FY 2025, according to its latest annual report, revenue reached nearly $7.1 million. This represented a decline of approximately 34.3% compared to the prior year. The company reported a net loss of roughly $216.2 million for the same period. This resulted in a negative net margin of approximately 3,050.4%, highlighting the intense research and development costs required to build and scale quantum processors.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was 0.0x. This ratio, which compares total debt to shareholder equity, indicates the company currently carries no debt on its books. The current ratio, measuring the ability to pay short-term bills with short-term assets, was approximately 37.4x. Free cash flow for FY 2025 was nearly negative $77.2 million. Free cash flow represents the cash a company generates after accounting for cash outflows to support operations and maintain its capital assets.
SoundHound creates voice-enabled AI software used in cars, restaurants, and smart devices. Its Houndify platform allows businesses to build natural conversational interfaces for their products. The company recently completed the acquisition of LivePerson, which helped integrate advanced customer engagement and agentic AI tools into its stack. SoundHound serves various sectors, including automotive and hospitality, through royalties and subscription contracts. Revenue is primarily derived from these long-term service contracts and the monetization of voice-enabled interactions.
In FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $168.9 million, an increase of approximately 99.4% over previous results. The company reported a net loss of roughly $14.0 million for the fiscal year. This narrowed its negative net margin to approximately 8.3%, indicating that the business is scaling its voice AI services more efficiently than in previous periods. This top-line growth reflects the increasing demand for conversational AI across enterprise and consumer markets.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was 0.0x. This indicates that the company has no total debt relative to its shareholder equity. The current ratio was roughly 4.6x, measuring the company's ability to cover its short-term debts with its short-term assets. Free cash flow for FY 2025 was approximately negative $103.1 million. This reflects the significant cash burn required to scale its software platform and integrate large acquisitions like LivePerson.
Rigetti faces risks as an early-stage company with significant accumulated deficits and a continued need for external capital to fund operations. There are substantial technological hurdles to achieving quantum advantage, and failing to meet development milestones could hurt investor confidence. High customer concentration is another factor, with much of its revenue coming from a few government entities and cloud partners. Global competition from well-funded sovereign programs and giant technology firms remains intense in the quantum space.
SoundHound deals with persistent cash burn as it scales its operations to compete in the crowded AI software market. The company faces significant execution risks following the integration of LivePerson, which could impact its financial stability if synergies are not realized. Competition from larger technology companies like Amazon or Microsoft presents ongoing pricing pressure and may limit market share. There are also potential regulatory hurdles regarding the use of generative AI technologies and data privacy concerns that could impact adoption.
Neither company currently has a positive Forward P/E based on future earnings estimates, so investors often look to the P/S ratio for comparison. The P/S ratio measures a stock's market value against its sales over the past twelve months.
Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.
Which stock would I buy in 2026?
I'd go with SoundHound AI, though neither company is a comfortable pick right now. Both are unprofitable and asking investors to bet on technologies still finding their commercial footing.
But SoundHound has something Rigetti is still working toward: a growing base of paying enterprise customers across healthcare, automotive, and restaurant industries. Revenue grew at a strong double-digit rate in the most recent quarter, the company raised its full-year outlook, and the voice AI platform is winning new enterprise customers across multiple industries.
Rigetti has made progress on its quantum hardware, and a CHIPS Act funding letter adds a layer of government validation. But revenue remains small, and the gap between its bookings momentum and actual recognized revenue is something investors need to understand before buying in.
Both stocks are speculative and carry significant risk. But SoundHound is closer to building a durable commercial business, and for a patient investor comfortable with early-stage volatility, that gives it a modest edge right now.

Rigetti Stock Is Down 49% This Year. Here’s What the Street’s Target Looks Like Now.
Rigetti Stock Is Down 49% This Year. Here's What the Street's Target Looks Like Now. ©ColiN00B from pixabay and Just_Super from Getty Images Signature via Canva
Rigetti Computing stock has fallen 49% over the past year, sliding from an intraday peak near $77 in early November 2025 to $16.01 as of September 23.
The stock carries 8 buy ratings, 1 outperform and 4 holds, with zero sells on the books right now. Separately, 12 analysts publish a price target, and their mean sits at $28.81, about 80% above the current price.
CEO Subodh Kulkarni sold 120,000 shares for $1.88 million on September 9 and CFO Jeffrey Bertelsen sold 25,000 shares for $375,010 on September 3, both selling into the same week Rigetti signed a $100 million federal quantum computing deal.
Analyst coverage on Rigetti stock has grown from 5 estimates a year ago to 12 today, and the Street kept its mean target above the stock price through nearly the entire stretch, even as the price itself cratered.
Rigetti Stock's Brutal Year Meets a $100 Million Government Lifeline
Rigetti Computing (RGTI) stock has lost 49% of its value over the past year, and the chart tells a story of a spike that gave almost all of it back. Shares touched roughly $77 in early November 2025 during the broader quantum computing rally, then spent the next ten months grinding lower to $16.01 by September 23.
The decline found a floor on September 8, when Rigetti signed a definitive $100 million agreement with the U.S. Department of Commerce to accelerate superconducting quantum computing research and development under the CHIPS Act. Shares jumped 7.2% that session, and rivals D-Wave and Quantinuum moved on similar CHIPS awards the same day, with Commerce taking a minority, non-controlling equity stake in Rigetti as a condition of the funding. The deal followed a Q2 report in which Rigetti posted a $28.1 million operating loss against revenue of just $5.1 million, still short of the $5.15 million analysts expected, so the federal award landed as the clearest positive catalyst the stock had seen since the crash began.
What complicates that read is timing. Kulkarni sold 120,000 shares at $15.68 on September 9, one day after the CHIPS news broke, cutting his direct stake to 140,411 shares. Bertelsen had already sold 25,000 shares at $15 on September 3, taking his stake to 168,067. Both exercised options at a fraction of the market price before selling, standard mechanics for executive compensation, but the sales still put insiders on the selling side of a stock the government just backed and the Street still rates a buy.
The government deal gives Rigetti stock a credibility floor it didn't have a month ago. Whether that floor holds depends on whether the company can convert federal R&D funding into the kind of deployment revenue that's been missing all year.
Why the Street Hasn't Walked Away From Rigetti Stock
Rigetti stock currently carries 8 buy ratings, 1 outperform rating and 4 holds, with no sell ratings on the books. Separately, 12 analysts publish a price target on the stock, and their mean sits at $28.81, which puts the target 80% above the September 23 close of $16.01.
RGTI Stock Street Analysts Target (TIKR)
That premium has been a constant through a wild year. Back on September 30, 2025, the stock itself briefly outran the Street, closing at $29.79 against a mean target of just $21.83, a rare stretch where the market priced Rigetti stock above what analysts thought it was worth. Once the pullback started, analysts didn't chase the price down. By December 31, the mean target had jumped to $38.24 even as the close fell to $22.15, and by March 31, 2026, with the stock at $14.04, the target still sat at $31.54, a gap of 225%.
The mean target has come off that high alongside the price, landing at $28.81 today, but the Street has held a buy-heavy stance through the entire round trip. Coverage has widened at the same time, from 5 analysts publishing targets a year ago to 12 now, which means more desks are willing to put a number on the stock, not fewer, even as the business itself keeps posting revenue misses.

Signs Definitive Agreement for $100M with U.S. Government to Accelerate R&D for Superconducting Quantum Computing
Rigetti announces that it has signed a definitive agreement with
the U.S. Department of Commerce for an award of $100 million to accelerate R&D projects addressing key technical challenges in scaling
and advancing superconducting quantum computers.
Berkeley, CA, September 8, 2026 -- Rigetti Computing, Inc.
(Nasdaq: RGTI) (“Rigetti” or the “Company”), a pioneer in full-stack quantum-classical computing, today announced
that its wholly owned subsidiary, Rigetti & Co, LLC, has signed a definitive agreement with the U.S. Department of Commerce (the
“Department”) for an award of $100 million in funding to accelerate superconducting quantum computing R&D.
The funding is allocated under the CHIPS Research and Development Office
Broad Agency Announcement pursuant to the CHIPS Act.
Under the agreement, Rigetti will pursue three R&D projects that
aim to address major technical bottlenecks in scaling superconducting quantum computing and will accelerate the Company’s roadmap
towards utility-scale quantum computing:
1.Compressing readout electronics into an integrated, miniaturized package
2.Expanding cryogenic capacity by orders of magnitude using a new cryostat architecture
3.Developing the fabrication capabilities for high-connectivity chip architectures
Quantum computing has tremendous promise to dramatically transform
critical areas including cryptography, chemistry, materials science, mathematical optimization, and AI/machine learning. Governments worldwide
are investing in this emerging technology given the national security and economic implications of quantum advantage.
“We are proud to be selected by the U.S. government to accelerate
R&D and progress against our roadmap to deliver commercially viable quantum computing capabilities,” says Dr. Subodh Kulkarni,
Rigetti CEO. “Solving crucial challenges in scaling gives us the opportunity to transform the industry by putting large-scale quantum
computers in the hands of America’s quantum computing researchers faster. Shortening the time to build quantum systems at scale
and reducing their cost will also allow for broader adoption, which will strengthen our domestic quantum computing ecosystem.”
The Department will receive a minority, non-controlling equity stake
in Rigetti as a condition for receiving the funds to enhance the return for the U.S. taxpayer.
Rigetti is a pioneer in full-stack quantum computing. Rigetti quantum
computers are based on superconducting qubits, which are widely believed to be the leading qubit modality given their maturity, clear
path to scaling, and fast gate speeds. Rigetti quantum computing systems achieve gate speeds of 50-70 nanoseconds, which is about 10,000
times faster than trapped-ion systems and 100 times faster than neutral-atom systems.
Rigetti sells on-premises 9-qubit to 108-qubit quantum computing systems,
which support national laboratories and quantum computing centers. Rigetti’s Cepheus 36-qubit to 108-qubit systems are based on
the Company’s proprietary chiplet-based technology and include the Company’s control electronics. Rigetti’s 9-qubit

D-Wave Quantum Inc. and the Supply Chain Management Research Center in the Sam M. Walton College of Business at the University of Arkansas (SCMRC) announced a collaboration to explore quantum computing?s impact on complex supply chain problems. In addition, D-Wave has joined the partnership program of the SCMRC, which currently has more than 25 industry partners. Supply chain decision-making often requires organizations to coordinate routes, inventory, facilities, schedules and workforce while balancing cost, speed, service and resilience.

Announced during CSCMP EDGE 2026, a leading conference and exhibition hosted by the Council of Supply Chain Management Professionals, the collaboration between D-Wave and the SCMRC will explore foundational and applied research in quantum optimization for a variety of supply chain use cases, including transportation routing, logistics network design, inventory and resource allocation, scheduling and decision-making under disruption. In addition, joint efforts may include curriculum and case development, student learning opportunities, engagement with industry, government and academic stakeholders and the development and sharing of practical frameworks and insights.

LOS ANGELES, CA - October 5, 2026 (NEWMEDIAWIRE) - D-Wave Quantum Inc. (NASDAQ: QBTS) ("D-Wave" or the "Company"), the only dual-platform quantum computing company providing both annealing and gate-model systems, software and services, recently launched its gate-model quantum computing simulator beta program, marking an important milestone in D-Wave's gate-model development roadmap.
The beta program offers select customers early access to the simulator in advance of its general availability to experiment with error-aware programming and develop quantum applications in preparation for D-Wave's forthcoming gate-model systems. The simulator is built around D-Wave's dual-rail superconducting gate-model technology, which is designed to harness error detection to deliver efficient quantum error correction with significantly lower hardware overhead as systems scale. Participants in the simulator beta program include commercial and research organizations: BBVA, FirstQFM, Florida Atlantic University (FAU) and the Julich Supercomputing Centre (JSC).

Quantum computing has gained increasing attention in recent years. Amid the technology's potential for exponentially faster computing, companies like Alphabet, IBM, and Nvidia have taken an interest in it.
Additionally, many smaller, pure-play quantum computing stocks have emerged, and two of the more prominent ones are IonQ (IONQ -1.83%) and D-Wave Quantum (QBTS -0.82%).
Although these stocks carry significant risks, their smaller sizes also offer greater potential for higher returns should they succeed. Thus, it is worth asking which of these stocks might be the better stock to buy.
Image source: The Motley Fool.
One limitation of quantum computing is that the technology is often error-prone. This means any company that can minimize that problem has a better chance of success, and IonQ may have the solution with its trapped-ion quantum system.
Last year, IonQ demonstrated 2-qubit gate fidelities of 99.99%. This technology unlocked more complex applications that could now be performed with minimal error rates. While that does not make it faster than its big-tech counterparts, it performs tasks with industry-leading precision.
Furthermore, the company, often called the "Nvidia of quantum," has formed a partnership with that company. Under the terms of the agreement, Nvidia will install the IonQ Superion 256 system at the Nvidia Accelerated Quantum Research Center. This will tie IonQ into Nvidia's ecosystem, which could give it a competitive advantage.

D-Wave Quantum is widening its push into logistics and defense research while preparing to host its flagship user conference in Asia next year, a twin offensive that lands as investors grow impatient for proof that quantum computing can generate recurring commercial revenue.
The Canadian quantum specialist used the CSCMP EDGE 2026 industry gathering to unveil a collaboration with the Supply Chain Management Research Center at the University of Arkansas. The partnership establishes a Quantum Supply Chain Initiative Support Fund, which will bankroll independent research, teaching programs and case studies across three priority fields: retail, transportation and national defense. Wall Street Wants Receipts, Not Roadmaps
Market reaction to the Arkansas announcement was muted. D-Wave shares (NASDAQ: QBTS) slipped 1.2 percent to EUR 13.85 in the session, extending a bruising run that has wiped 39 percent off the stock since the start of the year. In German trading the equity was quoted at EUR 14.20, well below its 200-day moving average of EUR 17.91 — a gap that underscores the downward pressure the shares have faced for months.
The sector-wide retreat came to a head last Friday, when quantum stocks came under heavy selling pressure amid industry-wide questions about valuations and persistent uncertainty over how quickly commercial adoption will arrive. For D-Wave, that headwind is arriving at an awkward moment, just as the company works to broaden its technological reach.
Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying D-Wave Quantum?
At the heart of the debate is a single question: when will technological partnerships translate into durable, growing revenue? Quantum computing spent years as a pure future bet with very long development cycles. Investors now demand tangible evidence of value in day-to-day industrial operations. Tie-ups with IT service providers demonstrate that established corporations are paying attention, but the decisive test is whether customers will commit to recurring software and cloud spending. Should that transition stall, the strain between heavy research budgets and hesitant bookings could erode investor confidence for good.
Not everyone sees near-term upside in optimization. Helmut Katzgraber of investment firm 55North recently argued that classical computing systems are likely to retain the upper hand in optimization tasks for the foreseeable future, pointing instead to materials and chemistry simulation as the more promising near-term opportunity for quantum machines.
Supporters point to D-Wave's steady opening of its product suite to new user groups. The company launched a gate-model simulator that grants selected organizations from industry and academia early access to tools for fault-tolerant programming. Participants include BBVA, FirstQFM, Florida Atlantic University and the Jülich Supercomputing Centre, with delivery running through the company's Leap cloud service and its Ocean SDK developer kit. The beta program, which began on a Thursday, lets testers work with applications built on Dual-Rail technology designed to detect errors at the hardware level.
The company also strengthened its leadership bench in technology and security. Bernard Gavgani, a technology and innovation adviser to the Group Executive Management of BNP Paribas and formerly the bank's CIO, joined the Board of Directors and the cybersecurity committee. That kind of network could accelerate acceptance of quantum architectures in finance and the corporate world — and if these initiatives convert into rising orders soon, a meaningful re-rating could follow.
The bear case rests on institutional caution that shows no sign of lifting. Friday's selloff illustrated how sensitive the entire sector is to doubts about profitability; without fresh corporate deals, the downtrend in the share chart could harden. A key risk lies in the length of customer onboarding: many industrial firms are still testing quantum approaches in pilot projects without releasing long-term budgets. If the broader market climate for unprofitable growth companies tightens, capital could become scarce.
The stock's path now hinges on concrete operational milestones. As long as the current annual low of EUR 11.12 holds, the broader recovery scenario for the quote remains intact; a sustained break below that mark under heavy selling would likely invite follow-on selling. Investors already have their next date circled: on October 28, 2026, D-Wave will host the Qubits Asia 2026 user conference in Seoul, where customers are expected to present real-world deployment reports and new research findings. Those presentations will reveal just how far practical industrial use has actually progressed.

D-Wave Quantum (QBTS) stock jumped about 5% in Wednesday premarket trading to roughly $18.47. The move followed the announcement of a strategic partnership with global IT services company CGI.
The agreement will bring D-Wave’s quantum computing technology into CGI’s services portfolio. The companies plan to target practical optimization problems across transportation, logistics and retail.
CGI will use D-Wave’s Advantage2 annealing quantum computer and hybrid solvers. The partnership builds on more than a year of work between the two companies.
CGI Opens Another Enterprise Route for D-Wave
Potential transportation applications include train scheduling, rail-network operations and resource allocation. Retail uses could include supply-chain planning, delivery routing and workforce scheduling.
The companies are also targeting industrial production planning, energy-grid optimization and asset maintenance. These are areas where D-Wave argues quantum annealing can complement classical computing.
That commercial focus is important because D-Wave is already trying to prove that quantum computing can solve real-world optimization problems today. Its technology differs from many quantum rivals focused mainly on longer-term gate-model machines.
D-Wave has previously highlighted work with AT&T where its technology reduced one network optimization workload from roughly one hour to under 15 seconds.
The CGI agreement could give D-Wave access to a much wider enterprise customer base. CGI employs roughly 94,000 professionals and maintains alliances with more than 150 technology companies.
D-Wave’s bookings have already accelerated. First-half 2026 bookings reached $35.5 million, up more than 1,120% year over year.
Remaining performance obligations reached $40.7 million, up 668% from a year earlier. More than 100 customers generated revenue during the first half.
Valuation and Cash Burn Remain the Big Risks
Revenue is still small compared with D-Wave’s valuation. Second-quarter revenue was just $3.1 million, essentially unchanged from a year earlier.
The company also recorded a $53.3 million operating loss during the quarter. Research and development spending alone reached $28.2 million.
D-Wave does have substantial funding available. It ended June with about $546 million in liquidity and recently finalized an agreement for up to $100 million from the U.S. Department of Commerce.
Still, continued losses mean future financing and dilution remain risks. Investors also need D-Wave to convert rapidly rising bookings into sustained revenue growth.
The CGI deal strengthens the company’s enterprise-commercialization story, but it does not disclose guaranteed revenue or contract value. The next test is whether partnerships like this translate into larger recurring customer deployments.

D-Wave Partners with University of Arkansas to Establish Quantum Supply Chain Initiative at the Sam M. Walton College of Business
Collaboration will facilitate education and research into quantum computing applications for supply chain challenges in retail, transportation and national defense
PALO ALTO, Calif. & FAYETTEVILLE, Ark., October 05, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--D-Wave Quantum Inc. (NASDAQ: QBTS) ("D-Wave"), the only dual-platform quantum computing company providing annealing and gate-model systems, software and services, and the Supply Chain Management Research Center in the Sam M. Walton College of Business at the University of Arkansas (SCMRC) today announced a collaboration to explore quantum computing's impact on complex supply chain problems. The collaboration establishes the Quantum Supply Chain Initiative Support Fund with the SCMRC, which is intended to advance thought leadership, education and independent research focused on the application of quantum computing to supply chain management across retail, transportation and national defense. In addition, D-Wave has joined the partnership program of the SCMRC, which currently has more than 25 industry partners.
Supply chain decision-making often requires organizations to coordinate routes, inventory, facilities, schedules and workforce while balancing cost, speed, service and resilience. As these networks become more complex and disruptions become more consequential, quantum and hybrid-quantum computing approaches are emerging to complement established methods.
Announced during CSCMP EDGE 2026, a leading conference and exhibition hosted by the Council of Supply Chain Management Professionals, the collaboration between D-Wave and the SCMRC will explore foundational and applied research in quantum optimization for a variety of supply chain use cases, including transportation routing, logistics network design, inventory and resource allocation, scheduling and decision-making under disruption. In addition, joint efforts may include curriculum and case development, student learning opportunities, engagement with industry, government and academic stakeholders and the development and sharing of practical frameworks and insights.
"Supply chains are highly dynamic, with decision-making that can have a far-reaching impact on efficiency and costs," said Murray Thom, vice president of quantum technology evangelism at D-Wave. "We're seeing quantum computing technologies emerge as potentially powerful alternatives to existing classical approaches. The Walton College is at the forefront of supply chain innovation, not only educating the next generation of supply chain professionals and conducting groundbreaking research, but also engaging industry to effect economic change. We're thrilled to support the College as it facilitates a quantum-ready supply chain."
"The Walton College is dedicated to exploring the very latest methods, processes and technologies that advance supply chain management and resilience," said Brian Fugate, Associate Dean for Research and Graduate Programs with Walton College. "Quantum computing is showing great potential to help organizations accelerate decision-making, mitigate disruption and drive better operational outcomes. We're excited to partner with D-Wave, one of the quantum computing industry's foremost leaders, to bring quantum into our research portfolio and ultimately benefit students and partners alike."
About the Sam M. Walton College of Business
The Sam M. Walton College of Business at the University of Arkansas is a nationally recognized leader in business education, known for innovative programs in supply chain management, entrepreneurship, finance and experiential learning. Located in the heart of one of the nation's most dynamic business regions, Walton College prepares students to lead with integrity, analytical rigor and entrepreneurial spirit.
As Arkansas' flagship institution, the U of A provides an internationally competitive education in more than 200 academic programs. Founded in 1871, the U of A contributes more than $3 billion to Arkansas' economy through the teaching of new knowledge and skills, entrepreneurship and job development, discovery through research and creative activity, while also providing training for professional disciplines. The Carnegie Foundation classifies the U of A among the few U.S. colleges and universities with the highest level of research activity. Quantum computing stocks are extending their recent rebound Thursday as investors continue to digest a series of technical developments across the industry. IonQ (NYSE:IONQ | IONQ Price Prediction) stock is up 4% to $44.08, while D-Wave Quantum (NYSE:QBTS) stock is gaining 3% to $17.23 and Rigetti Computing (NASDAQ:RGTI) stock is adding 2% to $16.28.
The gains come as the broader market is relatively steady, with the Defiance Quantum ETF (NYSE ARCA:QTUM) up 0.16% to $152.70 and the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE ARCA:SPY) up 0.07% to $768.36. IonQ has drawn particular attention after recent advances in quantum error correction and the planned deployment of its Superion 256 system at NVIDIA‘s (NASDAQ:NVDA) Accelerated Quantum Research Center.
IonQ’s Breakthrough Keeps Attention High
IonQ’s recent progress in quantum error correction is helping maintain buying interest after the company demonstrated a real-time decoder running on a standard CPU. IonQ says the development addresses a major bottleneck in fault-tolerant quantum computing by allowing errors to be corrected in real time without slowing execution.
The latest development follows IonQ’s introduction of its Superion 256 platform, giving investors another technical milestone to consider. IonQ also announced that Superion 256 will be the first quantum processor deployed at NVIDIA’s Accelerated Quantum Research Center, where the companies plan to study applications including financial modeling, materials science and drug discovery.
IonQ’s planned NVIDIA relationship could give the company additional visibility as researchers work on integrating quantum processors with advanced computing infrastructure. IonQ expects first customer deliveries of Superion 256 in 2027, making the system an important longer-term development rather than an immediate revenue driver.
For investors, the distinction between technical progress and commercial adoption remains important. IonQ’s recent announcements can strengthen the technology narrative, while sustained revenue growth and customer deployments could provide a clearer indication of how those advances translate into a commercial business.
D-Wave is also participating in the quantum-stock rebound, with D-Wave Quantum stock up 3% today. D-Wave’s approach differs from IonQ’s trapped-ion technology, giving investors exposure to a separate path toward commercial quantum applications.
Rigetti is gaining as well, with Rigetti stock up 2% to $16.28. Rigetti’s superconducting-qubit approach provides another distinct technology model, underscoring how investors are backing several competing architectures as the industry works toward more capable quantum systems.
The recent rebound has brought renewed attention to the broader quantum-computing group, although the sector remains highly sensitive to technical milestones and expectations for commercialization. Defiance Quantum ETF’s relatively small gain compared with the larger moves in IonQ, D-Wave Quantum and Rigetti shows that today’s buying is concentrated more heavily in individual names.
IonQ’s latest breakthroughs could keep attention focused on whether improvements in error correction and quantum-system performance can translate into useful commercial applications. Investors should watch for signs of customer adoption, deployments and recurring revenue across IonQ, D-Wave Quantum and Rigetti, while keeping position sizes modest given the industry’s ongoing technological and commercialization risks.

For years, quantum computing lived in a comfortable limbo on global financial markets: revolutionary on paper, commercially distant in practice. University research grants, academic lab setups and glossy future promises shaped how the entire sector was perceived. D-Wave Quantum is now showing what it looks like when that early phase starts to fade — and the market is not entirely convinced by the view.
The clearest signal of this maturation sits in the company's governance. On September 21, D-Wave appointed Bernard Gavgani to its Board of Directors and Cybersecurity Committee. Gavgani serves as Senior Advisor for Technology and Innovation to the BNP Paribas Group Executive Management, bringing expertise in global technology strategy, AI governance, cybersecurity and operational transformation. His arrival follows the August 17 addition of Kevan P. Krysler, CFO of Carbon Robotics, to the Board of Directors and Audit Committee. Krysler carries broad leadership experience in finance and corporate governance at both listed and private technology companies.
Profiles like these are not assembled for the next academic conference. They point toward the demands of large institutional customers, strict security reviews and robust control structures — the unglamorous machinery of enterprise sales.
Evidence that this professionalization is translating into day-to-day business comes from Japan. Telecommunications group NTT DOCOMO launched its second production quantum application built on D-Wave systems on August 18. The results are concrete: the application cut location registration signals during daily peak load by 65.3% and reduced paging signals by 7.0%.
Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying D-Wave Quantum?
That is a measurable relief in live mobile networks rather than a theoretical benchmark under lab conditions. The company is also shoring up its technological base and market access. A funding agreement with the U.S. Department of Commerce provides up to $100 million from the CHIPS and Science Act, directed at research and development of superconducting annealing and gate-model technologies. A strategic partnership with CGI adds the Advantage2 quantum computer and hybrid optimization tools to the service portfolio for corporate clients.
Despite these steps toward industrial anchoring, the trading floor remains cautious. The stock closed Friday at EUR 15.29, down 33% since the start of the year. That skepticism has a logic of its own: at a market capitalization equivalent to EUR 5.83 billion, little room exists for disappointment. Market participants want hard numbers, not feasibility demonstrations.
The hard numbers, so far, are thin. Analyst Craig Ellis of B. Riley Securities reaffirmed his buy rating on Monday and kept his price target at $40, with his confidence resting mainly on the medium-term potential of the computing architecture. S&P Global Market Intelligence noted that bookings could rise sharply this year — but also flagged that second-quarter revenue stalled at $3.1 million, flat year over year and short of expectations.
That gap is the core tension running through the stock. Growing bookings are a necessary precondition for future success, yet the exchange increasingly demands proof that those contracts convert reliably into actual revenue. Partnerships with established IT service providers such as CGI, aimed at unlocking concrete optimization projects in logistics and retail, are sensible moves to strengthen governance and open doors to large corporate customers. Still, every personnel or organizational realignment remains a promise about the future as long as the operating leverage fails to materialize.
The stock also sits a considerable distance from its 52-week high of EUR 40.41, a retreat that illustrates how quickly speculative goodwill evaporates when hard metrics lag behind hopes. D-Wave now faces the task of proving that operational efficiency gains in network operations can be converted into recurring, scalable revenue across the board. For investors, the decisive phase has begun: the era of pure future hope is giving way to an industrial trial by fire — one that favors those with a strong appetite for risk and plenty of patience.

There's a lot of buzz surrounding quantum computing stocks right now, and three of the most popular among investors are Rigetti Computing (RGTI -0.66%), D-Wave Quantum (QBTS -0.82%), and IonQ (IONQ -1.83%).
Their share prices have soared over the past three years, but most have lackluster sales, and rising costs mean that the jury is still out on their ability to survive over the long term.
So, let's take a quick look at what each company is doing to stay in the fight and which one looks best positioned to be here years from now.
Image source: Getty Images.
IonQ recently reported second-quarter revenue of $80.1 million, a 287% increase from the year-ago quarter. Part of that jump came from a recent acquisition of SkyWater Technology, a chip foundry business, but organic sales are on the rise, too.
IonQ's management says that organic quantum computing revenue will double this calendar year. That's impressive growth and shows that IonQ can attract commercial customers.
But investors should know that the company isn't profitable yet, and its losses are widening. IonQ's non-GAAP (adjusted) earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) loss was $120.3 million in the second quarter, much higher than its loss of $36.5 million in the year-ago quarter.
Still, IonQ has cash and cash equivalents of $3 billion, so there's little worry that the company will run out of money any time soon.

Rigetti is gaining customers, but commercial sales are lacking
Rigetti recently expanded its collaboration with Hewlett-Packard and the Pittsburgh Supercomputing Center, and its sales popped 185% in the second quarter.
The problem is that revenue was just $5.1 million, barely a blip on the company's own income statement. Investors should know that Rigetti's CEO, Subodh Kulkarni, has said that "commercial revenue remains early" and it's likely it could be several more years before its tech reaches a point where it's significant.
The good news for Rigetti is that the company is debt-free and has $541 million in cash to keep the lights on for a while.

D-Wave's bookings in the second quarter were impressive, soaring 1,120% to $35.5 million. That's a good sign that customers are interested in D-Wave's products and services, but revenue hasn't come as easily for the company.
D-Wave had sales of just $3.1 million in the quarter, below sales in the year-ago quarter, and its adjusted EBITDA loss was $37.1 million for the quarter.
D-Wave has about $588 million in cash and cash equivalents, which should give the company a substantial runway, but its lack of sales and significant losses should be a red flag for investors.

IonQ likely has the best shot at survival
The quantum computing market is just getting started, and it'll likely be a wild ride for a while. But IonQ has higher revenue than its peers, and its organic sales from its quantum computing business appear on track to increase significantly.
And, given its very strong cash position, IonQ has plenty of money to keep itself going for the foreseeable future.
But that doesn't mean investors should hit the buy button right now. IonQ's stock is very expensive, with a trailing price-to-sales (P/S) ratio of 57, which is far above the tech sector average of about 8.
It could take many more years for the commercial benefits of quantum computing to catch up to the technology's potential. Which means that investors buying IonQ or any quantum computing stock will have to wait a while to see how all of this plays out -- and likely endure significant share price volatility along the way.

Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying D-Wave Quantum?
For a company burning capital through a hardware-intensive development phase, that commitment provides rare planning certainty. It cushions the heavy R&D burden and reinforces the technological foundation needed to compete globally. Yet subsidies are a catalyst, not a cure. They can accelerate the maturation of the hardware and lay groundwork for future commercial platforms, but they cannot by themselves manufacture durable market success.
A study published Monday in the journal Quantum Information Processing adds a note of caution from the laboratory side. Researchers examined noise models on the Advantage2 system, a processor built on the Zephyr architecture with up to 7,440 qubits. Their finding: as problem sizes grow, chain strength scaling behaves less favorably than earlier theoretical models had assumed.
In practical terms, embedding complex optimization tasks consumes more correction resources than customers might expect. The physical characteristics of the hardware impose real limits on how far commercial applications can stretch — a reminder that the distance between a working qubit count and a working business case is measured in more than just engineering milestones.

That "if" carries the weight of everything above. Euphoria phases in the quantum sector alternate regularly with sober reassessments, and Monday's gain shows how receptive the space remains to positive catalysts. The decisive test for D-Wave is not a conference booth or a federal grant — it is whether quarterly revenue can return to growth. Until that happens, the stock will demand considerable risk tolerance from anyone who holds it.

D-Wave Partners with University of Arkansas to Establish Quantum Supply Chain Initiative At the Sam M. Walton College of Business
D-WAVE QUANTUM INC.
D-Wave Quantum Inc. and the Supply Chain Management Research Center in the Sam M. Walton College of Business at the University of Arkansas (SCMRC) announced a collaboration to explore quantum computing?s impact on complex supply chain problems. The collaboration establishes the Quantum Supply Chain Initiative Support Fund with the SCMRC, which is intended to advance thought leadership, education and independent research focused on the application of quantum computing to supply chain management across retail, transportation and national defense. In addition, D-Wave has joined the partnership program of the SCMRC, which currently has more than 25 industry partners. Supply chain decision-making often requires organizations to coordinate routes, inventory, facilities, schedules and workforce while balancing cost, speed, service and resilience.
As these networks become more complex and disruptions become more consequential, quantum and hybrid-quantum computing approaches are emerging to complement established methods. Announced during CSCMP EDGE 2026, a leading conference and exhibition hosted by the Council of Supply Chain Management Professionals, the collaboration between D-Wave and the SCMRC will explore foundational and applied research in quantum optimization for a variety of supply chain use cases, including transportation routing, logistics network design, inventory and resource allocation, scheduling and decision-making under disruption. In addition, joint efforts may include curriculum and case development, student learning opportunities, engagement with industry, government and academic stakeholders and the development and sharing of practical frameworks and insights.

D-Wave Launches Gate-Model Simulator Beta Program, Advancing Error-Aware Programming Capabilities
LOS ANGELES, CA - October 5, 2026 (NEWMEDIAWIRE) - D-Wave Quantum Inc. (NASDAQ: QBTS) ("D-Wave" or the "Company"), the only dual-platform quantum computing company providing both annealing and gate-model systems, software and services, recently launched its gate-model quantum computing simulator beta program, marking an important milestone in D-Wave's gate-model development roadmap.
The beta program offers select customers early access to the simulator in advance of its general availability to experiment with error-aware programming and develop quantum applications in preparation for D-Wave's forthcoming gate-model systems. The simulator is built around D-Wave's dual-rail superconducting gate-model technology, which is designed to harness error detection to deliver efficient quantum error correction with significantly lower hardware overhead as systems scale. Participants in the simulator beta program include commercial and research organizations: BBVA, FirstQFM, Florida Atlantic University (FAU) and the Julich Supercomputing Centre (JSC).
To view the full press release, visit https://ibn.fm/Dy07z
About D-Wave Quantum Inc.
D-Wave is a leader in the development and delivery of quantum computing systems, software, and services. It is the world's first commercial supplier of quantum computers, and the first and only to offer dual-platform quantum computing products and services, spanning both annealing and gate-model quantum computing technologies. D-Wave's mission is to help customers realize the value of quantum today through enterprise-grade systems available on-premises and via its LeapTM quantum cloud service, which offers 99.9% availability and uptime. More than 100 organizations across commercial, government and research sectors trust D-Wave to address complex computational challenges using quantum computing. Learn more about realizing the value of quantum computing today and how D-Wave is shaping the quantum-driven industrial and societal advancements of tomorrow: https://www.dwavequantum.com.

Quantum computing has gained increasing attention in recent years. Amid the technology's potential for exponentially faster computing, companies like Alphabet, IBM, and Nvidia have taken an interest in it.
Additionally, many smaller, pure-play quantum computing stocks have emerged, and two of the more prominent ones are IonQ (IONQ -1.83%) and D-Wave Quantum (QBTS -0.82%).
Although these stocks carry significant risks, their smaller sizes also offer greater potential for higher returns should they succeed. Thus, it is worth asking which of these stocks might be the better stock to buy.
Image source: The Motley Fool.
One limitation of quantum computing is that the technology is often error-prone. This means any company that can minimize that problem has a better chance of success, and IonQ may have the solution with its trapped-ion quantum system.
Last year, IonQ demonstrated 2-qubit gate fidelities of 99.99%. This technology unlocked more complex applications that could now be performed with minimal error rates. While that does not make it faster than its big-tech counterparts, it performs tasks with industry-leading precision.
Furthermore, the company, often called the "Nvidia of quantum," has formed a partnership with that company. Under the terms of the agreement, Nvidia will install the IonQ Superion 256 system at the Nvidia Accelerated Quantum Research Center. This will tie IonQ into Nvidia's ecosystem, which could give it a competitive advantage.
Unfortunately, such gains may not yet provide sufficient support for its financials. Its $145 million in revenue in the first half of 2026 was well above the $28 million in the same period a year ago, indicating it is growing faster than Nvidia. However, high operating expenses led to a $1.06 billion operating loss in the first two quarters of 2026, well above the $210 million loss from the same time frame last year.
$17BMarket cap calculated using publicly traded shares outstanding only. Does not include unlisted, private, or dual-class non-traded shares. Implied market cap may vary.
Moreover, IonQ stock is down by more than one-third over the last year. Despite that decline, it still has a price-to-sales (P/S) ratio of around 65, an indication that the company's fundamentals have little bearing on the stock price. Such a valuation makes it extremely difficult to forecast IonQ's near-term direction at this time.
Why investors might consider D-Wave Quantum
Nonetheless, investors might also find challenges amid the potential in D-Wave Quantum. In an industry where some have predicted commercial viability is years away, Leap's quantum cloud service already runs customer applications.
Additionally, it has become a leader in optimization, as its quantum annealing technology helps find solutions while analyzing millions of variables. For example, AT&T cut a one-hour task down to less than 15 seconds using this application.
Thus, it is likely not surprising that companies use its technology to retrain AI models, generate molecular structures, and lower energy consumption.
However, much like with IonQ, D-Wave Quantum is far from profitability. In the first half of 2026, revenue of $5.9 million fell 67% year over year, though a large system sale in early 2025 skewed these results. Also, high operating expenses led to a $66 million loss for the same period.
$5.9BMarket cap calculated using publicly traded shares outstanding only. Does not include unlisted, private, or dual-class non-traded shares. Implied market cap may vary.
Amid that financial performance, the stock dropped by almost 40% over the last year. Furthermore, at a P/S ratio of approximately 475, the stock's valuation factors in several years of anticipated revenue gains, making the stock a risky buy at this time.
Should investors buy IonQ or D-Wave Quantum?
As conditions stand now, both stocks face deep uncertainty in the foreseeable future, and risk-averse investors should probably avoid both of them. Nonetheless, if choosing one, I recommend IonQ.
Although D-Wave's success at applying the technology now is noteworthy, one cannot deny IonQ's built-in credibility that comes with its Nvidia partnership.
Moreover, while both are too expensive, it is less risky to pay around 65 times sales than it is to buy at a P/S ratio of around 475. Thus, amid significant uncertainty, IonQ looks like the safer buy that offers a higher probability of success.

IonQ Jumps 4% on BoA Buy Rating; Rigetti and D-Wave Quantum Gain 2%
Bank of America just placed a bold bet on the largest pure-play quantum stock by revenue, and the ripple effect lifted the entire sector. Here is what the analyst sees that has other investors scrambling to reassess their positions.
Published September 30, 2026, 11:05am ET · 3 min read
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
IonQ (NYSE:IONQ | IONQ Price Prediction) stock jumped 4% to $45.60 on Wednesday after Bank of America initiated coverage with a Buy rating and a $60 price target. Rigetti Computing (NASDAQ:RGTI) shares advanced 2% to $16.13, while D-Wave Quantum (NYSE:QBTS) stock also rose 2% to $16.84. The quantum computing group found support as investors digested the fresh analyst call on IonQ.
The Defiance Quantum ETF (NYSE ARCA:QTUM) gained 0.27% to $152.28. Broader markets moved higher, with the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE ARCA:SPY) up 0.66% to $769.24. Attention centered on IonQ’s revenue trajectory, hardware deployments, and commercial roadmap even as losses and execution risks remained in focus.
Bank of America highlighted IonQ as the largest public pure-play quantum company by revenue. The firm pointed to the company’s semiconductor-enabled path for scaling qubit counts along with broad customer engagement across quantum computing, communications, and sensing. Bank of America applied a blended enterprise-value-to-sales multiple to longer-term revenue projections that include both quantum hardware and foundry-related sales.
IonQ has expanded its reach through acquisitions that add nearer-term products and additional commercialization paths. The recent SkyWater deal in particular brought foundry capacity and helped lift the company’s fiscal 2026 revenue guidance midpoint. Losses continue as the industry works toward more reliable, error-corrected systems.
Rigetti stock participated in the session’s strength across the quantum group. The company develops superconducting quantum processors and related software platforms aimed at commercial and research users. Rigetti shares have remained volatile as investors weigh progress on hardware roadmaps against ongoing funding needs and competition.
D-Wave Quantum stock likewise posted a gain. D-Wave focuses on annealing-based quantum systems that target optimization problems for enterprise customers. Both Rigetti and D-Wave Quantum operate in a still-early commercial market where technical milestones and customer adoption remain central to valuation debates.
The Defiance Quantum ETF’s modest advance indicated that the day’s move was concentrated in the pure-play names rather than a broad sector surge. Quantum computing stocks have experienced sharp swings this year as investors balance long-term potential against the reality of current error rates and limited near-term revenue visibility. IonQ’s larger revenue base relative to peers has helped the company stand out in recent analyst coverage.
Similarities across IonQ, Rigetti, and D-Wave Quantum include heavy investment in research and development and dependence on continued capital markets access. Differences appear in technology approaches, with IonQ emphasizing trapped-ion systems, Rigetti pursuing superconducting circuits, and D-Wave Quantum specializing in quantum annealing.
Bank of America’s $60 target implies meaningful upside from current levels, though other firms carry a range of higher and lower objectives. Commercial adoption remains early because today’s qubits are still error-prone, and useful fault-tolerant machines are widely expected later in the decade. IonQ’s expanded foundry capabilities and Superion system plans for 2027 offer additional catalysts that investors will monitor closely.
Investors should consider keeping position sizes modest given the high volatility typical of quantum computing stocks and the execution risks that accompany ambitious hardware roadmaps. Progress on revenue growth and system reliability could support further gains, yet setbacks in either area may pressure shares across the group.

D-Wave Quantum is widening its push into logistics and defense research while preparing to host its flagship user conference in Asia next year, a twin offensive that lands as investors grow impatient for proof that quantum computing can generate recurring commercial revenue.
The Canadian quantum specialist used the CSCMP EDGE 2026 industry gathering to unveil a collaboration with the Supply Chain Management Research Center at the University of Arkansas. The partnership establishes a Quantum Supply Chain Initiative Support Fund, which will bankroll independent research, teaching programs and case studies across three priority fields: retail, transportation and national defense. Researchers intend to examine whether quantum algorithms can outpace classical methods in vehicle routing, logistics network control, inventory management and the allocation of scarce resources. A particular focus will fall on decision-making during acute supply disruptions.
Under the arrangement, D-Wave joins a partner program that already counts more than 25 industrial participants, giving the company a direct line to potential adopters in business and government. The move builds on a partnership announced roughly two weeks earlier with CGI Global covering transport and commerce solutions, and it sits alongside an agreement with the US Department of Commerce worth up to USD 100 million in funding through the CHIPS Act.
Wall Street Wants Receipts, Not Roadmaps
Market reaction to the Arkansas announcement was muted. D-Wave shares (NASDAQ: QBTS) slipped 1.2 percent to EUR 13.85 in the session, extending a bruising run that has wiped 39 percent off the stock since the start of the year. In German trading the equity was quoted at EUR 14.20, well below its 200-day moving average of EUR 17.91 — a gap that underscores the downward pressure the shares have faced for months.
The sector-wide retreat came to a head last Friday, when quantum stocks came under heavy selling pressure amid industry-wide questions about valuations and persistent uncertainty over how quickly commercial adoption will arrive. For D-Wave, that headwind is arriving at an awkward moment, just as the company works to broaden its technological reach.
Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying D-Wave Quantum?
At the heart of the debate is a single question: when will technological partnerships translate into durable, growing revenue? Quantum computing spent years as a pure future bet with very long development cycles. Investors now demand tangible evidence of value in day-to-day industrial operations. Tie-ups with IT service providers demonstrate that established corporations are paying attention, but the decisive test is whether customers will commit to recurring software and cloud spending. Should that transition stall, the strain between heavy research budgets and hesitant bookings could erode investor confidence for good.
Not everyone sees near-term upside in optimization. Helmut Katzgraber of investment firm 55North recently argued that classical computing systems are likely to retain the upper hand in optimization tasks for the foreseeable future, pointing instead to materials and chemistry simulation as the more promising near-term opportunity for quantum machines.
Supporters point to D-Wave's steady opening of its product suite to new user groups. The company launched a gate-model simulator that grants selected organizations from industry and academia early access to tools for fault-tolerant programming. Participants include BBVA, FirstQFM, Florida Atlantic University and the Jülich Supercomputing Centre, with delivery running through the company's Leap cloud service and its Ocean SDK developer kit. The beta program, which began on a Thursday, lets testers work with applications built on Dual-Rail technology designed to detect errors at the hardware level.
The company also strengthened its leadership bench in technology and security. Bernard Gavgani, a technology and innovation adviser to the Group Executive Management of BNP Paribas and formerly the bank's CIO, joined the Board of Directors and the cybersecurity committee. That kind of network could accelerate acceptance of quantum architectures in finance and the corporate world — and if these initiatives convert into rising orders soon, a meaningful re-rating could follow.
The bear case rests on institutional caution that shows no sign of lifting. Friday's selloff illustrated how sensitive the entire sector is to doubts about profitability; without fresh corporate deals, the downtrend in the share chart could harden. A key risk lies in the length of customer onboarding: many industrial firms are still testing quantum approaches in pilot projects without releasing long-term budgets. If the broader market climate for unprofitable growth companies tightens, capital could become scarce.
The stock's path now hinges on concrete operational milestones. As long as the current annual low of EUR 11.12 holds, the broader recovery scenario for the quote remains intact; a sustained break below that mark under heavy selling would likely invite follow-on selling. Investors already have their next date circled: on October 28, 2026, D-Wave will host the Qubits Asia 2026 user conference in Seoul, where customers are expected to present real-world deployment reports and new research findings. Those presentations will reveal just how far practical industrial use has actually progressed.

D-Wave Quantum (QBTS) Stock Gains as CGI Deal Targets Real-World Quantum Applications
D-Wave Quantum (QBTS) stock jumped 5% after CGI partnered with the company to offer quantum computing services across logistics, transport and retail.
By Trader EdgeSeptember 23, 20263 Mins Read
D-Wave Quantum stock was up about 5% in Wednesday premarket trading near $18.47.
CGI and D-Wave announced a strategic partnership covering logistics, transportation and retail.
CGI will integrate D-Wave’s Advantage2 quantum computer and hybrid solvers into its technology services.
D-Wave reported first-half bookings of $35.5 million, up more than 1,120% year over year.
The main risk remains valuation and cash burn, with second-quarter revenue still only $3.1 million.
D-Wave Quantum (QBTS) stock jumped about 5% in Wednesday premarket trading to roughly $18.47. The move followed the announcement of a strategic partnership with global IT services company CGI.
The agreement will bring D-Wave’s quantum computing technology into CGI’s services portfolio. The companies plan to target practical optimization problems across transportation, logistics and retail.
CGI will use D-Wave’s Advantage2 annealing quantum computer and hybrid solvers. The partnership builds on more than a year of work between the two companies.
CGI Opens Another Enterprise Route for D-Wave
Potential transportation applications include train scheduling, rail-network operations and resource allocation. Retail uses could include supply-chain planning, delivery routing and workforce scheduling.
The companies are also targeting industrial production planning, energy-grid optimization and asset maintenance. These are areas where D-Wave argues quantum annealing can complement classical computing.
That commercial focus is important because D-Wave is already trying to prove that quantum computing can solve real-world optimization problems today. Its technology differs from many quantum rivals focused mainly on longer-term gate-model machines.
D-Wave has previously highlighted work with AT&T where its technology reduced one network optimization workload from roughly one hour to under 15 seconds.
The CGI agreement could give D-Wave access to a much wider enterprise customer base. CGI employs roughly 94,000 professionals and maintains alliances with more than 150 technology companies.
D-Wave’s bookings have already accelerated. First-half 2026 bookings reached $35.5 million, up more than 1,120% year over year.
Remaining performance obligations reached $40.7 million, up 668% from a year earlier. More than 100 customers generated revenue during the first half.
Valuation and Cash Burn Remain the Big Risks
Revenue is still small compared with D-Wave’s valuation. Second-quarter revenue was just $3.1 million, essentially unchanged from a year earlier.
The company also recorded a $53.3 million operating loss during the quarter. Research and development spending alone reached $28.2 million.
D-Wave does have substantial funding available. It ended June with about $546 million in liquidity and recently finalized an agreement for up to $100 million from the U.S. Department of Commerce.
Still, continued losses mean future financing and dilution remain risks. Investors also need D-Wave to convert rapidly rising bookings into sustained revenue growth.
The CGI deal strengthens the company’s enterprise-commercialization story, but it does not disclose guaranteed revenue or contract value. The next test is whether partnerships like this translate into larger recurring customer deployments.
