Bank of America highlighted IonQ as the largest public pure-play quantum company by revenue. The firm pointed to the company’s semiconductor-enabled path for scaling qubit counts along with broad customer engagement across quantum computing, communications, and sensing. Bank of America applied a blended enterprise-value-to-sales multiple to longer-term revenue projections that include both quantum hardware and foundry-related sales.
IonQ has expanded its reach through acquisitions that add nearer-term products and additional commercialization paths. The recent SkyWater deal in particular brought foundry capacity and helped lift the company’s fiscal 2026 revenue guidance midpoint. Losses continue as the industry works toward more reliable, error-corrected systems.
Rigetti stock participated in the session’s strength across the quantum group. The company develops superconducting quantum processors and related software platforms aimed at commercial and research users. Rigetti shares have remained volatile as investors weigh progress on hardware roadmaps against ongoing funding needs and competition.
D-Wave Quantum stock likewise posted a gain. D-Wave focuses on annealing-based quantum systems that target optimization problems for enterprise customers. Both Rigetti and D-Wave Quantum operate in a still-early commercial market where technical milestones and customer adoption remain central to valuation debates.
The Defiance Quantum ETF’s modest advance indicated that the day’s move was concentrated in the pure-play names rather than a broad sector surge. Quantum computing stocks have experienced sharp swings this year as investors balance long-term potential against the reality of current error rates and limited near-term revenue visibility. IonQ’s larger revenue base relative to peers has helped the company stand out in recent analyst coverage.
Similarities across IonQ, Rigetti, and D-Wave Quantum include heavy investment in research and development and dependence on continued capital markets access. Differences appear in technology approaches, with IonQ emphasizing trapped-ion systems, Rigetti pursuing superconducting circuits, and D-Wave Quantum specializing in quantum annealing.
Bank of America’s $60 target implies meaningful upside from current levels, though other firms carry a range of higher and lower objectives. Commercial adoption remains early because today’s qubits are still error-prone, and useful fault-tolerant machines are widely expected later in the decade. IonQ’s expanded foundry capabilities and Superion system plans for 2027 offer additional catalysts that investors will monitor closely.
Investors should consider keeping position sizes modest given the high volatility typical of quantum computing stocks and the execution risks that accompany ambitious hardware roadmaps. Progress on revenue growth and system reliability could support further gains, yet setbacks in either area may pressure shares across the group.

D-Wave Quantum Illustration mit AI erstellt.
D-Wave Quantum is widening its push into logistics and defense research while preparing to host its flagship user conference in Asia next year, a twin offensive that lands as investors grow impatient for proof that quantum computing can generate recurring commercial revenue.
The Canadian quantum specialist used the CSCMP EDGE 2026 industry gathering to unveil a collaboration with the Supply Chain Management Research Center at the University of Arkansas. The partnership establishes a Quantum Supply Chain Initiative Support Fund, which will bankroll independent research, teaching programs and case studies across three priority fields: retail, transportation and national defense. Researchers intend to examine whether quantum algorithms can outpace classical methods in vehicle routing, logistics network control, inventory management and the allocation of scarce resources. A particular focus will fall on decision-making during acute supply disruptions.
Under the arrangement, D-Wave joins a partner program that already counts more than 25 industrial participants, giving the company a direct line to potential adopters in business and government. The move builds on a partnership announced roughly two weeks earlier with CGI Global covering transport and commerce solutions, and it sits alongside an agreement with the US Department of Commerce worth up to USD 100 million in funding through the CHIPS Act.
Wall Street Wants Receipts, Not Roadmaps
Market reaction to the Arkansas announcement was muted. D-Wave shares (NASDAQ: QBTS) slipped 1.2 percent to EUR 13.85 in the session, extending a bruising run that has wiped 39 percent off the stock since the start of the year. In German trading the equity was quoted at EUR 14.20, well below its 200-day moving average of EUR 17.91 — a gap that underscores the downward pressure the shares have faced for months.
The sector-wide retreat came to a head last Friday, when quantum stocks came under heavy selling pressure amid industry-wide questions about valuations and persistent uncertainty over how quickly commercial adoption will arrive. For D-Wave, that headwind is arriving at an awkward moment, just as the company works to broaden its technological reach.
Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying D-Wave Quantum?
At the heart of the debate is a single question: when will technological partnerships translate into durable, growing revenue? Quantum computing spent years as a pure future bet with very long development cycles. Investors now demand tangible evidence of value in day-to-day industrial operations. Tie-ups with IT service providers demonstrate that established corporations are paying attention, but the decisive test is whether customers will commit to recurring software and cloud spending. Should that transition stall, the strain between heavy research budgets and hesitant bookings could erode investor confidence for good.
Not everyone sees near-term upside in optimization. Helmut Katzgraber of investment firm 55North recently argued that classical computing systems are likely to retain the upper hand in optimization tasks for the foreseeable future, pointing instead to materials and chemistry simulation as the more promising near-term opportunity for quantum machines.
Supporters point to D-Wave's steady opening of its product suite to new user groups. The company launched a gate-model simulator that grants selected organizations from industry and academia early access to tools for fault-tolerant programming. Participants include BBVA, FirstQFM, Florida Atlantic University and the Jülich Supercomputing Centre, with delivery running through the company's Leap cloud service and its Ocean SDK developer kit. The beta program, which began on a Thursday, lets testers work with applications built on Dual-Rail technology designed to detect errors at the hardware level.
The company also strengthened its leadership bench in technology and security. Bernard Gavgani, a technology and innovation adviser to the Group Executive Management of BNP Paribas and formerly the bank's CIO, joined the Board of Directors and the cybersecurity committee. That kind of network could accelerate acceptance of quantum architectures in finance and the corporate world — and if these initiatives convert into rising orders soon, a meaningful re-rating could follow.
The bear case rests on institutional caution that shows no sign of lifting. Friday's selloff illustrated how sensitive the entire sector is to doubts about profitability; without fresh corporate deals, the downtrend in the share chart could harden. A key risk lies in the length of customer onboarding: many industrial firms are still testing quantum approaches in pilot projects without releasing long-term budgets. If the broader market climate for unprofitable growth companies tightens, capital could become scarce.
The stock's path now hinges on concrete operational milestones. As long as the current annual low of EUR 11.12 holds, the broader recovery scenario for the quote remains intact; a sustained break below that mark under heavy selling would likely invite follow-on selling. Investors already have their next date circled: on October 28, 2026, D-Wave will host the Qubits Asia 2026 user conference in Seoul, where customers are expected to present real-world deployment reports and new research findings. Those presentations will reveal just how far practical industrial use has actually progressed.

D-Wave Quantum (QBTS) Stock Gains as CGI Deal Targets Real-World Quantum Applications
D-Wave Quantum (QBTS) stock jumped 5% after CGI partnered with the company to offer quantum computing services across logistics, transport and retail.
By Trader EdgeSeptember 23, 20263 Mins Read
D-Wave Quantum stock was up about 5% in Wednesday premarket trading near $18.47.
CGI and D-Wave announced a strategic partnership covering logistics, transportation and retail.
CGI will integrate D-Wave’s Advantage2 quantum computer and hybrid solvers into its technology services.
D-Wave reported first-half bookings of $35.5 million, up more than 1,120% year over year.
The main risk remains valuation and cash burn, with second-quarter revenue still only $3.1 million.
D-Wave Quantum (QBTS) stock jumped about 5% in Wednesday premarket trading to roughly $18.47. The move followed the announcement of a strategic partnership with global IT services company CGI.
The agreement will bring D-Wave’s quantum computing technology into CGI’s services portfolio. The companies plan to target practical optimization problems across transportation, logistics and retail.
CGI will use D-Wave’s Advantage2 annealing quantum computer and hybrid solvers. The partnership builds on more than a year of work between the two companies.
CGI Opens Another Enterprise Route for D-Wave
Potential transportation applications include train scheduling, rail-network operations and resource allocation. Retail uses could include supply-chain planning, delivery routing and workforce scheduling.
The companies are also targeting industrial production planning, energy-grid optimization and asset maintenance. These are areas where D-Wave argues quantum annealing can complement classical computing.
That commercial focus is important because D-Wave is already trying to prove that quantum computing can solve real-world optimization problems today. Its technology differs from many quantum rivals focused mainly on longer-term gate-model machines.
D-Wave has previously highlighted work with AT&T where its technology reduced one network optimization workload from roughly one hour to under 15 seconds.
The CGI agreement could give D-Wave access to a much wider enterprise customer base. CGI employs roughly 94,000 professionals and maintains alliances with more than 150 technology companies.
D-Wave’s bookings have already accelerated. First-half 2026 bookings reached $35.5 million, up more than 1,120% year over year.
Remaining performance obligations reached $40.7 million, up 668% from a year earlier. More than 100 customers generated revenue during the first half.
Valuation and Cash Burn Remain the Big Risks
Revenue is still small compared with D-Wave’s valuation. Second-quarter revenue was just $3.1 million, essentially unchanged from a year earlier.
The company also recorded a $53.3 million operating loss during the quarter. Research and development spending alone reached $28.2 million.
D-Wave does have substantial funding available. It ended June with about $546 million in liquidity and recently finalized an agreement for up to $100 million from the U.S. Department of Commerce.
Still, continued losses mean future financing and dilution remain risks. Investors also need D-Wave to convert rapidly rising bookings into sustained revenue growth.
The CGI deal strengthens the company’s enterprise-commercialization story, but it does not disclose guaranteed revenue or contract value. The next test is whether partnerships like this translate into larger recurring customer deployments.

D-Wave Partners with University of Arkansas to Establish Quantum Supply Chain Initiative at the Sam M. Walton College of Business
Collaboration will facilitate education and research into quantum computing applications for supply chain challenges in retail, transportation and national defense
PALO ALTO, Calif. & FAYETTEVILLE, Ark., October 05, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--D-Wave Quantum Inc. (NASDAQ: QBTS) ("D-Wave"), the only dual-platform quantum computing company providing annealing and gate-model systems, software and services, and the Supply Chain Management Research Center in the Sam M. Walton College of Business at the University of Arkansas (SCMRC) today announced a collaboration to explore quantum computing's impact on complex supply chain problems. The collaboration establishes the Quantum Supply Chain Initiative Support Fund with the SCMRC, which is intended to advance thought leadership, education and independent research focused on the application of quantum computing to supply chain management across retail, transportation and national defense. In addition, D-Wave has joined the partnership program of the SCMRC, which currently has more than 25 industry partners.
Supply chain decision-making often requires organizations to coordinate routes, inventory, facilities, schedules and workforce while balancing cost, speed, service and resilience. As these networks become more complex and disruptions become more consequential, quantum and hybrid-quantum computing approaches are emerging to complement established methods.
Announced during CSCMP EDGE 2026, a leading conference and exhibition hosted by the Council of Supply Chain Management Professionals, the collaboration between D-Wave and the SCMRC will explore foundational and applied research in quantum optimization for a variety of supply chain use cases, including transportation routing, logistics network design, inventory and resource allocation, scheduling and decision-making under disruption. In addition, joint efforts may include curriculum and case development, student learning opportunities, engagement with industry, government and academic stakeholders and the development and sharing of practical frameworks and insights.
"Supply chains are highly dynamic, with decision-making that can have a far-reaching impact on efficiency and costs," said Murray Thom, vice president of quantum technology evangelism at D-Wave. "We're seeing quantum computing technologies emerge as potentially powerful alternatives to existing classical approaches. The Walton College is at the forefront of supply chain innovation, not only educating the next generation of supply chain professionals and conducting groundbreaking research, but also engaging industry to effect economic change. We're thrilled to support the College as it facilitates a quantum-ready supply chain."
"The Walton College is dedicated to exploring the very latest methods, processes and technologies that advance supply chain management and resilience," said Brian Fugate, Associate Dean for Research and Graduate Programs with Walton College. "Quantum computing is showing great potential to help organizations accelerate decision-making, mitigate disruption and drive better operational outcomes. We're excited to partner with D-Wave, one of the quantum computing industry's foremost leaders, to bring quantum into our research portfolio and ultimately benefit students and partners alike."
About the Sam M. Walton College of Business
The Sam M. Walton College of Business at the University of Arkansas is a nationally recognized leader in business education, known for innovative programs in supply chain management, entrepreneurship, finance and experiential learning. Located in the heart of one of the nation's most dynamic business regions, Walton College prepares students to lead with integrity, analytical rigor and entrepreneurial spirit.
As Arkansas' flagship institution, the U of A provides an internationally competitive education in more than 200 academic programs. Founded in 1871, the U of A contributes more than $3 billion to Arkansas' economy through the teaching of new knowledge and skills, entrepreneurship and job development, discovery through research and creative activity, while also providing training for professional disciplines. The Carnegie Foundation classifies the U of A among the few U.S. colleges and universities with the highest level of research activity. U.S. News & World Report ranks the U of A among the top public universities in the nation. See how the U of A works to build a better world at Arkansas Research and Economic Development News.
About D-Wave Quantum Inc.
D-Wave is a leader in the development and delivery of quantum computing systems, software, and services. It is the world's first commercial supplier of quantum computers, and the first and only to offer dual-platform quantum computing products and services, spanning both annealing and gate-model quantum computing technologies. D-Wave's mission is to help customers realize the value of quantum today through enterprise-grade systems available on-premises and via its Leap™ quantum cloud service, which offers 99.9% availability and uptime. More than 100 organizations across commercial, government and research sectors trust D-Wave to address complex computational challenges using quantum computing. Investors often weigh the risks of unproven but transformative technologies. Comparing D-Wave Quantum (QBTS -0.82%) and QuantumScape (QS +1.09%) highlights the choice between quantum computing and advanced battery storage for your long-term portfolio.
D-Wave is an early leader in commercial quantum computing, already generating revenue from global enterprises. QuantumScape is focused on perfecting solid-state batteries to disrupt the automotive industry but remains in the pre-revenue phase. Both companies represent high-stakes bets on scientific breakthroughs, making them frequent points of comparison for growth-oriented investors.
D-Wave provides quantum computing systems and cloud-based services designed to solve complex business problems. Its customer base includes prominent names such as Mastercard (MA +2.23%), Pfizer (PFE -1.40%), and Siemens Healthineers (SEMHF -1.84%). A partnership with CGI (GIB +1.24%) helps bring these quantum solutions to the logistics and retail sectors within the evolving tech stocks landscape.
In its latest annual report, filed for FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $24.6 million, representing growth of roughly 178.5% over the previous year. The company reported a net loss of approximately $355.1 million, leading to a negative net margin of about -1,444.1%. This growth trajectory is a key factor for the P/S ratio, which compares the stock price to sales over the past twelve months.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was approximately 0.1x, which compares total debt to shareholder equity. The current ratio reached nearly 42.4x, which shows how easily a company can pay its short-term bills with its current assets. Free cash flow, or cash from operations minus capital spending, was negative $75.8 million for the year.
QuantumScape aims to redefine the battery industry by developing solid-state lithium-metal cells for electric vehicles. Its primary focus is on commercializing this technology alongside Volkswagen (VLKPF -5.06%), its most significant industrial partner. The company also recently highlighted a multi-year agreement with Honda to evaluate its battery performance for future vehicle models.
In FY 2025, the company recorded revenue of $0.0 because its products are still in the prototype and testing phases. Without revenue, it reported a net loss of nearly $435.1 million during the same fiscal period. Net margin, which tracks how much of each sales dollar remains after expenses, is not currently applicable for the business while it remains pre-revenue.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio was roughly 15.9x, indicating a substantial cash cushion to fund development. Its debt-to-equity ratio was approximately 0.1x, meaning total debt remains low compared to the value provided by its shareholders. Free cash flow for the fiscal year was negative $278.8 million, reflecting the high costs of building out its testing facilities.
D-Wave Quantum faces significant risks stemming from its status as an early-stage company with a history of substantial net losses. It must also compete with massive resources from firms like Microsoft (MSFT +1.48%), Amazon (AMZN -0.05%), and Intel (INTC -2.63%). The 2026 acquisition of Quantum Circuits adds complexity to its operational integration and technological roadmap.
QuantumScape is navigating the technical challenges of moving its battery technology from the lab to commercial production lines. The company is heavily dependent on its relationship with Volkswagen, making it vulnerable to strategy changes at its primary partner. Its capital-intensive business model may also require more funding, which could lead to shareholder dilution in the future.
D-Wave provides a clearer valuation path via its sales, while neither company currently has the positive future earnings estimates required for a Forward P/E ratio.
Valuation metrics sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.
Which stock would I buy in 2026?
I'd go with QuantumScape, though it is worth saying upfront that both of these are genuine moonshot stocks. They’re early-stage, unprofitable, and years from commercial scale. Anyone buying either one should understand they are making a speculative bet, not a conventional long-term investment.
D-Wave has paying customers, which sounds encouraging. But its revenue has barely moved in nearly two years while operating costs have surged dramatically. That means the business is burning through cash at a rate that makes its current valuation difficult to justify, even compared to a pre-revenue company.
QuantumScape's solid-state battery technology is still years from the automotive assembly line, and the timeline keeps stretching. But the company carries a substantial cash cushion that gives it real runway to get there without immediately needing to raise more money.
Between these two long shots, the one with more financial runway and a cleaner path to its first major commercial milestone seems like the more comfortable place to start.

IonQ Rises 4% as Post-Breakthrough Buying Continues; D-Wave Quantum Gains 3%, Rigetti Adds 2%
Quantum computing stocks are climbing again as a fresh wave of technical breakthroughs reshapes what investors think these companies can actually deliver, and the gap between hype and commercial reality has never mattered more.
Published September 24, 2026, 1:14pm ET · 3 min read
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
A close-up view of an IonQ quantum computing chip, representing the intricate technology at the heart of the company's ambitious valuation. Tonight's earnings report will shed light on the growth trajectory of this cutting-edge hardware. © Courtesy of IonQ
Quantum computing stocks are extending their recent rebound Thursday as investors continue to digest a series of technical developments across the industry. IonQ (NYSE:IONQ | IONQ Price Prediction) stock is up 4% to $44.08, while D-Wave Quantum (NYSE:QBTS) stock is gaining 3% to $17.23 and Rigetti Computing (NASDAQ:RGTI) stock is adding 2% to $16.28.
The gains come as the broader market is relatively steady, with the Defiance Quantum ETF (NYSE ARCA:QTUM) up 0.16% to $152.70 and the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE ARCA:SPY) up 0.07% to $768.36. IonQ has drawn particular attention after recent advances in quantum error correction and the planned deployment of its Superion 256 system at NVIDIA‘s (NASDAQ:NVDA) Accelerated Quantum Research Center.
IonQ’s Breakthrough Keeps Attention High
IonQ’s recent progress in quantum error correction is helping maintain buying interest after the company demonstrated a real-time decoder running on a standard CPU. IonQ says the development addresses a major bottleneck in fault-tolerant quantum computing by allowing errors to be corrected in real time without slowing execution.
The latest development follows IonQ’s introduction of its Superion 256 platform, giving investors another technical milestone to consider. IonQ also announced that Superion 256 will be the first quantum processor deployed at NVIDIA’s Accelerated Quantum Research Center, where the companies plan to study applications including financial modeling, materials science and drug discovery.
IonQ’s planned NVIDIA relationship could give the company additional visibility as researchers work on integrating quantum processors with advanced computing infrastructure. IonQ expects first customer deliveries of Superion 256 in 2027, making the system an important longer-term development rather than an immediate revenue driver.
For investors, the distinction between technical progress and commercial adoption remains important. IonQ’s recent announcements can strengthen the technology narrative, while sustained revenue growth and customer deployments could provide a clearer indication of how those advances translate into a commercial business.
D-Wave is also participating in the quantum-stock rebound, with D-Wave Quantum stock up 3% today. D-Wave’s approach differs from IonQ’s trapped-ion technology, giving investors exposure to a separate path toward commercial quantum applications.
Rigetti is gaining as well, with Rigetti stock up 2% to $16.28. Rigetti’s superconducting-qubit approach provides another distinct technology model, underscoring how investors are backing several competing architectures as the industry works toward more capable quantum systems.
The recent rebound has brought renewed attention to the broader quantum-computing group, although the sector remains highly sensitive to technical milestones and expectations for commercialization. Defiance Quantum ETF’s relatively small gain compared with the larger moves in IonQ, D-Wave Quantum and Rigetti shows that today’s buying is concentrated more heavily in individual names.
IonQ’s latest breakthroughs could keep attention focused on whether improvements in error correction and quantum-system performance can translate into useful commercial applications. Investors should watch for signs of customer adoption, deployments and recurring revenue across IonQ, D-Wave Quantum and Rigetti, while keeping position sizes modest given the industry’s ongoing technological and commercialization risks.

D-Wave Quantum Illustration mit AI erstellt.
For years, quantum computing lived in a comfortable limbo on global financial markets: revolutionary on paper, commercially distant in practice. University research grants, academic lab setups and glossy future promises shaped how the entire sector was perceived. D-Wave Quantum is now showing what it looks like when that early phase starts to fade — and the market is not entirely convinced by the view.
The clearest signal of this maturation sits in the company's governance. On September 21, D-Wave appointed Bernard Gavgani to its Board of Directors and Cybersecurity Committee. Gavgani serves as Senior Advisor for Technology and Innovation to the BNP Paribas Group Executive Management, bringing expertise in global technology strategy, AI governance, cybersecurity and operational transformation. His arrival follows the August 17 addition of Kevan P. Krysler, CFO of Carbon Robotics, to the Board of Directors and Audit Committee. Krysler carries broad leadership experience in finance and corporate governance at both listed and private technology companies.
Profiles like these are not assembled for the next academic conference. They point toward the demands of large institutional customers, strict security reviews and robust control structures — the unglamorous machinery of enterprise sales.
Evidence that this professionalization is translating into day-to-day business comes from Japan. Telecommunications group NTT DOCOMO launched its second production quantum application built on D-Wave systems on August 18. The results are concrete: the application cut location registration signals during daily peak load by 65.3% and reduced paging signals by 7.0%.
Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying D-Wave Quantum?
That is a measurable relief in live mobile networks rather than a theoretical benchmark under lab conditions. The company is also shoring up its technological base and market access. A funding agreement with the U.S. Department of Commerce provides up to $100 million from the CHIPS and Science Act, directed at research and development of superconducting annealing and gate-model technologies. A strategic partnership with CGI adds the Advantage2 quantum computer and hybrid optimization tools to the service portfolio for corporate clients.
Despite these steps toward industrial anchoring, the trading floor remains cautious. The stock closed Friday at EUR 15.29, down 33% since the start of the year. That skepticism has a logic of its own: at a market capitalization equivalent to EUR 5.83 billion, little room exists for disappointment. Market participants want hard numbers, not feasibility demonstrations.
The hard numbers, so far, are thin. Analyst Craig Ellis of B. Riley Securities reaffirmed his buy rating on Monday and kept his price target at $40, with his confidence resting mainly on the medium-term potential of the computing architecture. S&P Global Market Intelligence noted that bookings could rise sharply this year — but also flagged that second-quarter revenue stalled at $3.1 million, flat year over year and short of expectations.
That gap is the core tension running through the stock. Growing bookings are a necessary precondition for future success, yet the exchange increasingly demands proof that those contracts convert reliably into actual revenue. Partnerships with established IT service providers such as CGI, aimed at unlocking concrete optimization projects in logistics and retail, are sensible moves to strengthen governance and open doors to large corporate customers. Still, every personnel or organizational realignment remains a promise about the future as long as the operating leverage fails to materialize.
The stock also sits a considerable distance from its 52-week high of EUR 40.41, a retreat that illustrates how quickly speculative goodwill evaporates when hard metrics lag behind hopes. D-Wave now faces the task of proving that operational efficiency gains in network operations can be converted into recurring, scalable revenue across the board. For investors, the decisive phase has begun: the era of pure future hope is giving way to an industrial trial by fire — one that favors those with a strong appetite for risk and plenty of patience.

There's a lot of buzz surrounding quantum computing stocks right now, and three of the most popular among investors are Rigetti Computing (RGTI -0.66%), D-Wave Quantum (QBTS -0.82%), and IonQ (IONQ -1.83%).
Their share prices have soared over the past three years, but most have lackluster sales, and rising costs mean that the jury is still out on their ability to survive over the long term.
So, let's take a quick look at what each company is doing to stay in the fight and which one looks best positioned to be here years from now.
Image source: Getty Images.
IonQ recently reported second-quarter revenue of $80.1 million, a 287% increase from the year-ago quarter. Part of that jump came from a recent acquisition of SkyWater Technology, a chip foundry business, but organic sales are on the rise, too.
IonQ's management says that organic quantum computing revenue will double this calendar year. That's impressive growth and shows that IonQ can attract commercial customers.
But investors should know that the company isn't profitable yet, and its losses are widening. IonQ's non-GAAP (adjusted) earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) loss was $120.3 million in the second quarter, much higher than its loss of $36.5 million in the year-ago quarter.
Still, IonQ has cash and cash equivalents of $3 billion, so there's little worry that the company will run out of money any time soon.

Rigetti is gaining customers, but commercial sales are lacking
Rigetti recently expanded its collaboration with Hewlett-Packard and the Pittsburgh Supercomputing Center, and its sales popped 185% in the second quarter.
The problem is that revenue was just $5.1 million, barely a blip on the company's own income statement. Investors should know that Rigetti's CEO, Subodh Kulkarni, has said that "commercial revenue remains early" and it's likely it could be several more years before its tech reaches a point where it's significant.
The good news for Rigetti is that the company is debt-free and has $541 million in cash to keep the lights on for a while.

D-Wave's bookings in the second quarter were impressive, soaring 1,120% to $35.5 million. That's a good sign that customers are interested in D-Wave's products and services, but revenue hasn't come as easily for the company.
D-Wave had sales of just $3.1 million in the quarter, below sales in the year-ago quarter, and its adjusted EBITDA loss was $37.1 million for the quarter.
D-Wave has about $588 million in cash and cash equivalents, which should give the company a substantial runway, but its lack of sales and significant losses should be a red flag for investors.
$5.9BMarket cap calculated using publicly traded shares outstanding only. Does not include unlisted, private, or dual-class non-traded shares. Implied market cap may vary.
IonQ likely has the best shot at survival
The quantum computing market is just getting started, and it'll likely be a wild ride for a while. But IonQ has higher revenue than its peers, and its organic sales from its quantum computing business appear on track to increase significantly.
And, given its very strong cash position, IonQ has plenty of money to keep itself going for the foreseeable future.
But that doesn't mean investors should hit the buy button right now. IonQ's stock is very expensive, with a trailing price-to-sales (P/S) ratio of 57, which is far above the tech sector average of about 8.
It could take many more years for the commercial benefits of quantum computing to catch up to the technology's potential. Which means that investors buying IonQ or any quantum computing stock will have to wait a while to see how all of this plays out -- and likely endure significant share price volatility along the way.

With the Quantum World Congress set to open Wednesday, Wall Street's quantum bulls are making their case once more. B. Riley Securities analyst Craig Ellis has reaffirmed his buy rating on D-Wave Quantum and kept a $40 price target on the stock, arguing that U.S. quantum policy is shifting from pure research funding toward commercial deployment.
That thesis deserves scrutiny. The enthusiasm surrounding quantum computing's technological promise has, for now, papered over a far less inspiring financial picture at the company itself.
D-Wave's second-quarter 2026 results tell the story plainly. Revenue came in at just $3.1 million, well short of the $4.02 million consensus estimate. Strip out an earlier system sale, and the top line has effectively stood still for two years. Bookings did rise 59% in the quarter, but a durable, high-volume business has yet to materialize.
Pioneering science earns respect. In public markets, though, what counts is the ability to convert technology into dependable revenue. As long as corporate customers treat quantum machines as test-bed experiments rather than production tools, the commercial foundation remains uncomfortably thin.
Spending Outpaces Growth by a Wide Margin
While sales stall, costs are surging. GAAP operating expenses jumped 93% year over year in the second quarter to $54.98 million, and the adjusted EBITDA loss widened to $37.1 million. The January completion of the Quantum Circuits acquisition is among the items weighing on the numbers.
Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying D-Wave Quantum?
The strain on the balance sheet is considerable. Free cash flow burned through $79 million in the first half of 2026, and cash plus marketable securities fell by $273.1 million over twelve months to $546.2 million. News that CFO John Markovich stepped down in early September — with Greg Golkov taking over on an interim basis — does little to inspire confidence in the company's financial stewardship.
Management's Hopes Rest on Year-End System Sales
D-Wave's leadership is now pointing to the fourth quarter. CEO Alan Baratz has flagged meaningful revenue growth ahead from the planned sale of two annealing systems.
Such deals, however, are lumpy one-off events rather than a substitute for recurring income. And the company does not expect fault-tolerant machines with 100 logical qubits until 2032 — a painfully long stretch for a technology that is already consuming substantial capital.
The shares changed hands at EUR 15.32 on the day of the primary report, down 32% since the start of the year and 62% below their 52-week high. A separate reading put the stock at EUR 15.31 in European trading, a modest 0.7% daily decline, following a bounce earlier in the week. The 52-week peak stands at EUR 40.41.
Investors weighing the reiterated recommendation should read it carefully. The B. Riley note offers neither fresh revenue estimates nor an updated fundamental valuation. The firm also discloses that it expects compensation for investment-banking services from D-Wave within a three-month window. No specific new funding commitments or company-level catalysts were cited as the trigger for the rating.
At current levels, the equity remains above all a speculative wager on the industrial adoption of quantum computers. The pivotal question is whether D-Wave can use the upcoming congress to demonstrate genuine commercial momentum and measurable market traction.
Until the company reins in its heavy cash outflows and proves it can generate predictable revenue, conference headlines and analyst endorsements offer little support for a lasting turnaround.

Quantum Stocks Near Q3 Finish Line: How IONQ, RGTI & QBTS Are Faring
The quantum-computing industry is approaching the end of the third quarter with a striking disconnect. Commercial and technological progress has accelerated while pure-play quantum stocks have struggled to sustain their earlier valuations. IonQ IONQ, Rigetti Computing RGTI and D-Wave Quantum QBTS have all announced significant developments since reporting second-quarter results, yet their shares have remained highly sensitive to concerns about the pace of commercialization and interest rate-related updates.
The broader backdrop has not been particularly supportive. The Federal Reserve raised the federal funds target range to 3.75%-4% on Sept. 16, while its September projections put the median year-end 2026 rate at 4.1%, above the 3.8% projection in June. Meanwhile, August CPI rose 3.4% year over year, with core CPI up 2.4%. These conditions keep financing costs and discount rates elevated for companies whose cash flows remain heavily weighted toward the future.
Q3 Brings Policy Support Despite Tough Macro Conditions
The quarter has nevertheless produced stronger government support for quantum commercialization. On Sept. 8, the Commerce Department finalized up to $100 million in CHIPS R&D awards each for Rigetti and D-Wave, targeting superconducting quantum technologies, fabrication and packaging. The Department of Energy subsequently launched its Quantum Genesis Q Competition, with up to $215 million in planned funding to accelerate fault-tolerant quantum systems, alongside another $45 million testbed initiative.
The industry also gained a new public-market benchmark. Quantinuum completed its traditional IPO in the second quarter, raising $1.7 billion, and entered the third quarter with $2.1 billion in cash and short-term investments as of June 30. Its second-quarter revenues rose 279% year over year to $8 million. In September, it finalized another $100 million CHIPS award. The combination of an IPO, fresh capital and government-backed manufacturing programs indicates that funding for quantum development remains available even as investors become more selective.
How Quantum Stocks Are Progressing in Q3
IonQ: It enters the final stretch of the third quarter with a significant change in its financial outlook. It completed the SkyWater acquisition on July 31, adding semiconductor manufacturing and advanced packaging capabilities to its quantum platform. On Sept. 8, IonQ updated its 2026 revenue outlook to $450-$460 million, including SkyWater's contribution from the acquisition date through year-end.
The company also launched its Superion 256 platform, with first customer deliveries expected in 2027. On Sept. 23, IonQ announced that a Superion 256 system is scheduled to be installed at NVIDIA's Accelerated Quantum Research Center in 2027 and connected to NVIDIA's GB200 NVL72 infrastructure.
The quality of IonQ's Q3 performance will largely hinge on whether its expanded manufacturing capabilities, Superion 256 launch and strategic partnerships begin translating into stronger commercial momentum and revenue growth. This Zacks Rank #4 (Sell) stock has declined 17.3% so far during the third-quarter months. D-Wave: It approaches the quarter-end with a key focus on converting its strong booking pipeline into reported revenues. First-half bookings reached $35.5 million, up 1,120% year over year, while production applications accounted for 37.3% of first-half QCaaS revenues. The company also received up to $100 million in CHIPS R&D funding and reported a Nature-published advance involving its superconducting dual-rail architecture and quantum error correction.
These developments strengthen its longer-term technology and funding position, but third-quarter revenues and customer conversion will remain important indicators of whether the booking momentum is translating into financial performance. This Zacks Rank #4 stock has declined 28.5% so far during the third-quarter months. However, the Zacks Consensus Estimate for third-quarter 2026 bottom line is pegged at a loss of 9 cents per share, indicating a 78.1% improvement year over year.
Rigetti: Its third-quarter story has centered more on government-backed technology investment and commercialization infrastructure than near-term revenue acceleration. The Commerce Department finalized up to $100 million in CHIPS R&D funding for the company in September, supporting superconducting quantum-computing development, including fabrication and related technologies. Rigetti also established a dedicated Systems Delivery organization in August to scale on-premises customer deployments. With $541.3 million in cash and investments as of June 30, the company has resources to advance its roadmap.
Rigetti's third-quarter results will largely depend on whether its increased investment in technology and deployment capabilities begins to translate into stronger customer activity and revenue growth. D-Wave Quantum Illustration mit AI erstellt.
D-Wave Quantum closed Monday's session at EUR 15.44, a gain of 3.7% that rode a broad wave of enthusiasm across the quantum computing sector. The uptick offered a rare bright spot for a stock that has surrendered 32% since the start of the year — a decline that tells a more complicated story than any single trading day can.
At the heart of that story sits a widening gap between the company's technological ambitions and the commercial results it is currently delivering. For the first six months of 2026, D-Wave booked revenue of USD 5.9 million, down sharply from USD 18.1 million in the same period a year earlier — a 67% contraction. The second quarter alone brought in USD 3.08 million, falling short of the consensus estimates analysts had penciled in.
Those figures land with particular force given the company's valuation. D-Wave still trades at a very high price-to-sales multiple, and it carries a substantial net loss for fiscal 2025 alongside a low debt load. When a stock is priced for hypergrowth, any stumble in revenue expansion cuts deep. The market's patience is not infinite, and the recent numbers have tested it.
A Federal Commitment Worth Up to $100 Million
Against that commercial backdrop, Washington has stepped in with a meaningful vote of confidence. Roughly a week ago, the US Department of Commerce finalized a definitive agreement under the CHIPS and Science Act, granting D-Wave access to funding of up to USD 100 million. The money is earmarked for research and development, specifically to advance superconducting quantum systems spanning both annealing and gate-based models.
Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying D-Wave Quantum?
For a company burning capital through a hardware-intensive development phase, that commitment provides rare planning certainty. It cushions the heavy R&D burden and reinforces the technological foundation needed to compete globally. Yet subsidies are a catalyst, not a cure. They can accelerate the maturation of the hardware and lay groundwork for future commercial platforms, but they cannot by themselves manufacture durable market success.
A study published Monday in the journal Quantum Information Processing adds a note of caution from the laboratory side. Researchers examined noise models on the Advantage2 system, a processor built on the Zephyr architecture with up to 7,440 qubits. Their finding: as problem sizes grow, chain strength scaling behaves less favorably than earlier theoretical models had assumed.
In practical terms, embedding complex optimization tasks consumes more correction resources than customers might expect. The physical characteristics of the hardware impose real limits on how far commercial applications can stretch — a reminder that the distance between a working qubit count and a working business case is measured in more than just engineering milestones.
D-Wave is not waiting for the physics to sort itself out. Starting tomorrow, the company takes the floor at the Quantum World Congress 2026 in College Park, Maryland, running through September 25. The three-day event gives D-Wave a platform to present its systems, software, and specific applications to a technical audience.
A second date looms on October 28, 2026, when the company hosts Qubits Asia 2026 in Seoul — a full-day user conference designed to spotlight concrete customer deployments. Both events matter because investors increasingly want proof that quantum architectures can measurably speed up real workflows, not just theoretical benchmarks.
D-Wave Quantum at a turning point? This analysis reveals what investors need to know now.
Alongside its public-facing push, D-Wave has adjusted its board. On Friday, the company appointed Bernard Gavgani as an independent Class II director, and he will also sit on the board's cybersecurity committee. The move signals how prominently data security and governance now figure as quantum systems edge closer to commercial networks.
Sell-side opinion remains, for now, constructive. The analyst consensus stands at "Moderate Buy" with an average price target of USD 36.27 — a level that implies substantial upside if the company can right the ship.
That "if" carries the weight of everything above. Euphoria phases in the quantum sector alternate regularly with sober reassessments, and Monday's gain shows how receptive the space remains to positive catalysts. But the overarching trend is a reminder that patience is the market's scarcest commodity. The decisive test for D-Wave is not a conference booth or a federal grant — it is whether quarterly revenue can return to growth. Until that happens, the stock will demand considerable risk tolerance from anyone who holds it.

D-Wave Quantum, University of Arkansas to Collaborate on Quantum Computing's Supply Chain Application
D-Wave Quantum (QBTS) said Monday it will collaborate with the Sam M. Walton College of Business at the University of Arkansas to explore quantum computing's impact on supply chain problems.
The collaboration will establish the Quantum Supply Chain Initiative Support Fund at the Supply Chain Management Research Center, the company said. Financial terms were not disclosed.
D-Wave and the research center will explore supply chain uses for quantum computing including "transportation routing, logistics network design, inventory and resource allocation, scheduling and decision-making under disruption," the company said.

Quantum computing has gained increasing attention in recent years. Amid the technology's potential for exponentially faster computing, companies like Alphabet, IBM, and Nvidia have taken an interest in it.
Additionally, many smaller, pure-play quantum computing stocks have emerged, and two of the more prominent ones are IonQ (IONQ -1.83%) and D-Wave Quantum (QBTS -0.82%).
Although these stocks carry significant risks, their smaller sizes also offer greater potential for higher returns should they succeed. Thus, it is worth asking which of these stocks might be the better stock to buy.
Image source: The Motley Fool.
One limitation of quantum computing is that the technology is often error-prone. This means any company that can minimize that problem has a better chance of success, and IonQ may have the solution with its trapped-ion quantum system.

This will tie IonQ into Nvidia's ecosystem, which could give it a competitive advantage.
Unfortunately, such gains may not yet provide sufficient support for its financials. Its $145 million in revenue in the first half of 2026 was well above the $28 million in the same period a year ago, indicating it is growing faster than Nvidia. Walton College of Business at the University of Arkansas (SCMRC) announced a collaboration to explore quantum computing?s impact on complex supply chain problems. The collaboration establishes the Quantum Supply Chain Initiative Support Fund with the SCMRC, which is intended to advance thought leadership, education and independent research focused on the application of quantum computing to supply chain management across retail, transportation and national defense. In addition, D-Wave has joined the partnership program of the SCMRC, which currently has more than 25 industry partners. Supply chain decision-making often requires organizations to coordinate routes, inventory, facilities, schedules and workforce while balancing cost, speed, service and resilience. Announced during CSCMP EDGE 2026, a leading conference and exhibition hosted by the Council of Supply Chain Management Professionals, the collaboration between D-Wave and the SCMRC will explore foundational and applied research in quantum optimization for a variety of supply chain use cases, including transportation routing, logistics network design, inventory and resource allocation, scheduling and decision-making under disruption. In addition, joint efforts may include curriculum and case development, student learning opportunities, engagement with industry, government and academic stakeholders and the development and sharing of practical frameworks and insights. In addition, D-Wave has joined the partnership program of the SCMRC, which currently has more than 25 industry partners. Supply chain decision-making often requires organizations to coordinate routes, inventory, facilities, schedules and workforce while balancing cost, speed, service and resilience.
As these networks become more complex and disruptions become more consequential, quantum and hybrid-quantum computing approaches are emerging to complement established methods. Announced during CSCMP EDGE 2026, a leading conference and exhibition hosted by the Council of Supply Chain Management Professionals, the collaboration between D-Wave and the SCMRC will explore foundational and applied research in quantum optimization for a variety of supply chain use cases, including transportation routing, logistics network design, inventory and resource allocation, scheduling and decision-making under disruption. In addition, joint efforts may include curriculum and case development, student learning opportunities, engagement with industry, government and academic stakeholders and the development and sharing of practical frameworks and insights.
